title: The Shepherd and the Slanderer
english: Almsgiving purifies the passion while acquiring love; and the poor man is trained to be humble through his poverty.
Four generations of wisdom: fear of the Lord, wealth, glory, and life. 'These are the generations of Noah' (Gen 5:32), 'these are the generations of Abraham' (Gen 11:10).

Thorns and snares in crooked paths; but he who guards his own soul will escape them (Prov 2:18). And the Lord says to Adam: 'the earth shall bring forth for you thorns and thistles' (Gen 3:18), that is, the soul. Thorns and thistles he calls the sins, from which even the crown of Christ was struck; for he himself bore the sin of the world.

The rich shall rule the poor, and servants shall lend to their own masters (Prov 22:4). In the age to come, those enriched in every way in all knowledge and all wisdom shall rule over the unclean and those deprived of this wealth.
But who are the servants and who are the masters? It is not necessary now to publish this, because the word concerning them is mystical and deeper.
God blesses a cheerful and giving man (Prov 22:8a); but the Lord brings to completion the vanity of his works through virtue and knowledge (Prov 22:8b).

The one giving gifts acquires victory and honor (Prov 22:9a), but his soul is taken away from what he has possessed. The gifts of a man are called virtues, through which, conquering the devil, he offers himself as an honor to God, and his soul is taken away from the demons who had possessed it.

'Cast out a pestilence from the council, and strife shall come out with him' (Prov 22:10); for when he sits in a council, he dishonors all. He spoke of the most critical state, from which the wise Solomon wishes to cast out the man through spiritual teaching; and the strife signifies contention. He may also mean a pestilence and the devil, whom it is necessary to drive away from the soul. For if he sits in it, through impurity he dishonors all the righteous thoughts. And the apostle also shows the soul as a council, into which he introduces accusing thoughts and defending ones; 'for, he says, among one another, thoughts are either accusing or defending' (2 Cor 1:24 allusion); where there is accusation and defense, there is also a council.
A king shall rule with his lips (Prov 22:11); and the eyes of the Lord shall preserve perception (Prov 22:12); but the lawless one makes words contemptible.

The Lord himself is the shepherd of our souls and through spiritual knowledge he shepherds us, a knowledge which he who transgresses his law despises. It should be noted that since Christ is king, he is said to shepherd us through his condescension; 'for I,' he says, 'am the good shepherd' (John 10:11). But if he is a king among kings and a shepherd of sheep, he will at some time be only a king, as a dignity for those sheep who have transitioned into the kingdom.

The enemy, the devil, is seen to say: 'a lion in the roads, and murderers in the streets' (Prov 28:1); our enemy the devil prowls about like a lion seeking someone to devour, whom the sluggard, fearing him, rises up to meet in the work of virtues.
'A deep pit, the mouth of the lawless' (Prov 22:13); but he who is hated by the Lord will fall into it. Job, not being hated by the Lord, but on account of testing, fell into it (Job 5:7).
'Folly spreads from the heart of a youth; but a rod and instruction are far from him' (Prov 22:15); far from the heart of the foolish is the rod which is from the root of Jesse (Isa 11:1).

'The slanderer's poverty does many of his own evils; but he gives to the rich upon less' (Prov 14:4); just as the devil slanders us, taking from us the virtues which he did not give to us, so also we slander him, taking from him the evils which we did not give to him. And just as we take from him the evils, as if from a poor man we take in virtues; so also we give our virtues to him at a loss, as if to a rich man we give in evil. One of the elders was saying that we are the slanderers, slandering Christ, having made him poor through us, even though he owes nothing to us, and taking much from him and giving to Satan upon the humiliation of our souls.

'Compare your ear with the words of the wise and hear my word; and examine your own heart, so that you may know that they are good' (Prov 23:23); this one hears the words of God, the one doing the things commanded by them; 'for not the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified' (James 1:22).

'And you also shall write them down for yourself thrice for counsel and knowledge upon the breadth of your heart'; he who broadens his heart through purity will perceive the words of God, both the practical, the natural, and the theological. For all the...

title: Exegesis of Proverbs
english: According to the Scripture, the matter is divided quite sharply into the ethical, the natural, and the theological. To the first follows Proverbs, to the second Ecclesiastes, and to the third the Hymns of the Hymns.

Regarding Proverbs 24:8, 26: 'Do not give yourself as a surety, being ashamed of your face'; and 24:27: 'For if you do not have [something] from which to spread [it], the layer under your sides shall be taken.' Those who entertain bad thoughts and thus honor the evil one should strive to whatever power they can through good thoughts to restore the bad ones. For if they are not able to do this, the layer under the sides of the soul—that is, virtue—shall be taken. For this is called the garment of the mind when it stands in righteousness, but it is called a cushion when the rest has fallen due to bad thoughts.

Regarding Proverbs 24:28: 'Do not move the eternal boundaries which your fathers set.' He who moves the boundaries of godliness demonstrates either superstition or impiety, and he who moves the boundaries of courage achieves either rashness or cowardice. Likewise, this should be considered regarding the other virtues, regarding the dogmas, and regarding faith itself. Above all, this must be observed concerning the Holy Trinity; for he who does not theologize divides the Holy Spirit by baptism, and he who names others as gods introduces a crowd of gods.

Regarding Proverbs 23:1: 'If you sit to dine at the table of a powerful man, observe mindfully what is set before you...' and 23:3: 'But if you are more gluttonous, do not desire his delicacies'; for these things possess a false life. For not everyone contains the more mystical intellect of the Scripture. It is necessary that the Divine Scripture be understood mindfully and spiritually; for sensory knowledge according to the history is not true.

Regarding Proverbs 23:6: 'Do not dine with a coarse man'; nor desire his foods; 23:7: 'For in whatever way anyone swallows hair, so he eats and drinks'; 23:8: 'Nor let him be brought to you, and eat your bread with him'; for he will vomit him out and will defile your beautiful words. If the coarse man eats the grain of impiety and drinks lawless wine, one must not dine with him; therefore, it is not right to be impious and lawless, for these vices defile spiritual knowledge. Regarding Proverbs 23:9: 'Say nothing into the ears of a fool'...

Regarding the acquisition of your wise words: 'Say nothing wise,' that is to say, profound and mystical; for it is not fitting to cast pearls before swine. Regarding the boundaries: 'Do not shift the eternal boundaries which your fathers set,' and 'Do not enter the estate of orphans,' for wickedness is that by which they were deprived of their Father in heaven.

Regarding jealousy: 'Let not your heart envy sinners,' but be in the fear of the Lord all your days. Since it is said, 'All turns away from evil by the fear of the Lord' (Proverbs 23:17), it rightly exhorts us to turn away from all evil throughout our whole life.

Regarding offspring: 'If you keep these, you shall have offspring,' and 'your hope shall not be disappointed.' The mind has said that the right reasonings and the spiritual contemplations are offspring. Therefore, the soul is barren which does not have these offspring, which it is nature to bring forth from the spiritual bridegroom.

Regarding drunkenness and fornication: 'Every drunkard and fornicator shall be poor, and shall clothe himself in torn and ragged things.' There is no wedding garment that is torn and ragged. Regarding the mother: 'Listen, son, to the father of him who begot you, and do not despise that your mother has grown old.' One of the elders heard someone saying the soul is the mother of the mind; for this, he says, leads the mind into light through the practical virtues. The 'soul' referred to was the passionate part of the soul, which is divided into spirit and desire. For through courage and temperance, he says, we acquire wisdom and knowledge of God. Courage and temperance are the virtues of spirit and desire.

Regarding wines: 'Not of those who intoxicate with wines? Not of those who track where the drinking takes place?' These wines are from the vine of Sodom. Regarding fellowship: 'Do not get drunk with wine, but converse with righteous men, and converse in your walkings.' The Mind, conversing in walkings, walks worthily of the calling wherewith he was called.

Regarding eyes and cups: 'If you give your eyes to bowls and cups.' Sin resembles a bowl according to thought, and a cup according to energy. Regarding nakedness: 'Later you will walk more naked than the proud.' The proud knock much and do not open the place they knock at. But to the disciples the Lord says, 'Knock and it shall be opened to you' (Matthew 7:7). Regarding the eyes and mouth: 'Your eyes, when they see something foreign, your mouth then will speak.'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Judgment and the Sword of God
english: A scholion: A mind having received an alien thought will meditate on evil logismoi (thoughts). But he who guards himself will inherit life (Prov 26:3).
And it will lie still, just as in the heart of a sea, and just as a pilot in a great swell, being tossed by every wind of instruction (Prov 26:4).
When will the dawn be, so that coming, I may seek with those with whom I will be gathered? The dawn of the soul is the recognition of sin (Prov 26:5).
After steering comes war, but help comes with a deliberative heart. Those shipwrecking regarding faith do not fight against the opposing spirits in war with steering (Prov 26:6).

It is also possible to say this regarding every virtue; for there is also shipwreck regarding temperance, and regarding love, and regarding freedom from greed; and regarding each doctrine, similarly, it becomes a shipwreck according to the catholic and apostolic church. If, however, one must fight against the adversaries after steering, life upon the earth is near to us as a naval battle (Prov 26:7).
Wisdom and good understanding in the gates of the wise (Prov 26:9). The gates of the wise are the practical virtues through which the wisdom of God enters.

Impurity will stain a man like a plague (Prov 26:10), in a day of evil and in a day of tribulation, until it fails away. If vice diminishes virtue, and showing that virtue corrupts vice; this indeed will happen in the age to come, until vice fails away. For it has been set to stain instead of corrupting; but impurity is corrupted, either by practical [discipline] or by the punishment of severity (Prov 26:11).

To rescue those being led unto death and those being driven out to be slain, let him not spare. This is the word for those being made worthy of knowledge and those neglecting instruction, many of whom are led by vice unto death (Prov 26:13).

Eat honey, O son, for it is a good thing, so that your throat may be sweetened (Prov 25:28). He who benefits from the divine writings eats honey; but he who casts out the words from those very things from which even the holy prophets and apostles have received, chews wax. And to eat honey is possible for everyone who wishes, but the wax is for the pure alone (Prov 24:15).

Do not bring near the impious thinking they are righteous, nor be deceived by the fullness of the belly. Do not betray God for the sake of pleasure; for this one is thought to be righteous and will never abandon you (Prov 24:17). If the [man] falls...

Do not rejoice over your enemy, nor exult in his stumbling, for the Lord will see and it will not please him, and he will turn his anger away from him. God indeed turns his anger away from the fallen one having had mercy on him, but he is angry with the one who has become proud over the fall of his enemy.

For everyone who rejoices over a perishing soul is like the devil, who does not want all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. It should be noted, however, that he spoke of a human being here, for whom the Lord has enjoined us to pray in the Gospels (1 Timothy 2:1).

Evil offspring will not be produced, but the light of the ungodly will be extinguished. Bad virtues and doctrines will not be produced—for these are the offspring of the soul—because they do not fear the Lord; but those who are in the fear of the Lord will have offspring all day long, and their hope will not fail.

Fear God, son, and the King, and do not disobey either of them, 'so that they may know you, the only true God, and whom you sent, Jesus Christ' (John 4:24). For the ungodly will be extinguished suddenly; and who will know the punishments of both? How then does the Savior say in the Gospels: 'The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son' (John 5:22)? Either punishment is one thing, and judgment is another. Punishment is indeed the deprivation of impassibility and the knowledge of God with bodily distress; but judgment is the distribution of an age according to each of the rational bodies.

The tongue of a king is a sword and not a flesh-wound; and whoever is delivered to it will be crushed, 'and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God' (Ephesians 6:17). The 'not flesh-wound' [refers to] the 'not sensible'. If his anger is sharpened, he consumes men with nerves.

The sword of God consumes the old men who are being corrupted according to the desires of sickness, so that, having laid aside the old man, they may put on the new one created according to God. It rattles the bones of men and burns like a flame, 'for I came to cast fire upon the earth' (Luke 12:49). He is spotless for the pure, the one having been cleansed by the Lord and abstaining from all evil.
